promptHtml: Lesson 8.1's model of a path, with a slower one beside it: an inverter that takes 12 ns, from q1 to d3, on a 10 ns clock. Another of level 2's flip-flops, ff3, takes d3 at each rising edge. Cycles 0 and 1 are drawn for you. Set q3 for the rest.
explanationHtml: q1 changes at the edges that start cycles 2, 6 and 10, and d3 changes 12 ns later, 2 ns after the next edge. That edge comes too soon to take the new value, so ff3 takes it one edge later: q3 changes in cycles 4 and 8, and would in cycle 12, after the window. A path that takes longer than the period arrives late.

promptHtml: ff1 and ff2 are two flip-flops on one clock, with logic between ff1's Q and ff2's D. Put in order what happens on this path when it meets the setup time.
explanationHtml: A path starts at an edge, and ff1's Q changes a short time after it, never at the same instant. The new value then takes as long as the logic and the wires take, and it must be at ff2's D a setup time before the next edge for ff2 to take it there. The tempting slip is to put the setup time after the edge: setup comes before the edge, hold after it.
steps: A clock-to-output time later, ff1's Q changes.
The change passes through the logic and the wires.
It reaches ff2's D, at least a setup time before the next edge.
At the next rising edge, ff2 takes the new value.

promptHtml: msum16 keeps the last 16 samples in a chain of registers, x, each taking the one before at every edge, and adds them up into y. Vivado checks hold on every path as well as setup. Below is the start of the hold check of the path with the least time to spare: where it starts (Source), where it ends (Destination), how long its data takes, and Logic Levels, the number of cells of logic between the two.
explanationHtml: Read Logic Levels: 0. The path runs from x_reg[6][8] straight into x_reg[7][8], one register of the chain into the next, with only a wire between: 0.197 ns in all. The shortest paths come closest to breaking hold, because their new value arrives soonest after the edge. This one still arrives 0.121 ns later than hold needs: the Slack line at the top. Path Type names the check: Hold, worked out for the chip at its fastest (Min at Fast Process Corner), where data arrives soonest.

promptHtml: Lesson 8.1's model of a path, later in the same run: an inverter from q1 to d2, on a 10 ns clock, with d2 drawn. ff2 takes d2 at each rising edge. Set q2 for every cycle.
explanationHtml: d2 changes 6 ns after each change of q1, 4 ns before the next edge. So ff2 takes each new value at the first edge after q1 changed: q2 changes in cycles 2, 6 and 10, one cycle after q1.

promptHtml: Below is the Design Timing Summary of level 4's tick_led, built for the board. WNS is the setup check's smallest time to spare (lesson 7.2); WHS, further along the row, is the hold check's.
explanationHtml: Read WHS: 0.099. It is positive, so every path's new value arrives after the hold time is over, if only just, and the line under the table says every constraint is met. A negative WHS would mean a path so short that it changes a flip-flop's D too soon after the edge.
